title: Fuel a Future:
title_q: “We Never Ask Students What They Want”
title_short: Fuel a Future · National Challenge film (16:9)
format: 16:9 only · 1920×1080 (event film, plays on the big screen in the room)
headline: School rarely asks students what they want. NFTE starts with that question, measures the mindset it builds, and is joining forces with BUILD, because no student should feel they don't have what it takes.
story: An event film for the room: students, educators and donors. The hook is the system's problem, said by J.D.: so much of what students get is unconnected from what they want. NFTE begins with the opposite question: who are you? Young people build real businesses out of problems they care about, take agency over learning, and NFTE measures that mindset.

The turn is the merger, said out loud. J.D.: NFTE is merging and partnering with others, with BUILD students on screen, then BUILD says its own name. The button is urgent: no student should ever feel they don't have what it takes, and that is our problem, not theirs. The end card says Fuel a Future with both logos.

Loops: L1 What do students want? opens at 0:00 and closes at 00:17 on Who are you?. L2 Who fixes it? opens at the turn (01:00) and closes on the button. Hopeful and urgent, never adults talking down to kids.
do: Open on a student mid-pitch with the hook text on screen at frame 1.
Lower third on J.D.'s first on-camera line only (00:12).
BUILD students on screen under the merging line, and BUILD said once, from the merger video.
Mix for a room: dialogue loud and clear, music under it.
End on J.D.'s face for the last words, then the new end card.
dont: No city or one-event framing on screen; no readable place on slides, signs or the stage backdrop.
No crochet pitch slides with numbers in a tight shot (A36A7830: do not use it).
Don't caption the 22:18 fragment (“problem-side”) without checking the audio.
Never write “merger”: he says “merging and partnering”.
No second aspect ratio. No black frames, no fade from or to black.

transcript:
The pitch-competition sit-down (J.D. LaRock, 8 May 2026) is the Interview_Closeup_Audio_Edit.mp4 section. Line times come from output.json (no word times for this clip). Speaker labels were wrong and are removed: every answer is J.D.; lines that start with Q: are the interviewer. The machine wrote "Nifty"; it is written NFTE here, as he says it. Only the first 5 minutes and 20:00 to the end are here.
--- Interview_Closeup_Audio_Edit.mp4 ---
[00:04.4] Q: How does NFTE reflect where education is heading, not just where it's been?
[00:10.8] NFTE reflects where education is heading because NFTE is about entrepreneurship.
[00:18.3] Entrepreneurship is fundamentally about creation.
[00:22.3] Education needs sorely now to head in the direction of cultivating students' creative capabilities in a world of artificial intelligence, in a world of changing professions and changing industries, in a world where the traditional methods are not producing the academic achievement results that students need, and we all can see it, the world and students most of all need something different.
[00:51.2] NFTE's here not just to spread the gospel of entrepreneurship education, we are now here to reinvent education for what it needs to be, but frankly, what it always should have been.
[01:04.6] And that's what NFTE is about.
[01:07.0] Q: And what does learning by doing unlock for students?
[01:12.3] Learning by doing, first of all, unlocks the fact that students want to do things.
[01:19.8] People want to do things.
[01:22.2] Young people do not want to sit all the time in a classroom and hear about theoretical, conceptual things.
[01:32.2] They want to have a purpose in the world.
[01:35.4] They want to find out who they're about.
[01:38.8] And learning by doing allows young people to do those things.
[01:43.0] [do not use: transcription error]
[01:44.2] Q: As NFTE approaches its 40th anniversary in 2027, how do these ideas reflect the organization's enduring relevance, and what do they say about NFTE's role in shaping the future of education?
[01:59.5] NFTE's enduring relevance over 40 years comes from the fact that the world is full of businesses.
[02:05.8] You can't have a world without them.
[02:07.4] You can't have an economy without them.
[02:09.2] You can't have a community without them.
[02:11.5] And so the fact that we've stood for the idea that entrepreneurship education should be in American schools and schools globally is what we have always stood for. [do not use: names a place; NFTE wants national, evergreen cuts]
[02:23.8] But now we're taking that concept even further.
[02:27.0] We truly believe that we are not only teaching the entrepreneurial mindset, which is really applicable to jobs and careers that most people will have, whether they're small business owners or not.
[02:40.0] We also believe that, again, it's time now to unleash the creative capabilities that human beings have so we can power our world forward in a healthy way and in a way that actually drives individual prosperity and family prosperity, but also individual success and fulfillment.
[02:59.7] The NFTE model is about unleashing what's within young people so that they can become who they truly are and show the world all of the fantastic things that they can give it.
[03:11.5] Q: What do you consistently see in NFTE students that's often missing in traditional classroom settings?
[03:19.7] What I see in NFTE students that's missing from traditional classroom settings is the opportunity to take agency over learning and to do that by presenting learning.
[03:31.9] We stand up in front of so many talented students around the country and around the world who are seventh graders, eighth graders, ninth graders, tenth graders.
[03:42.2] We're even working more with younger children now.
[03:44.8] They stand up there.
[03:46.5] You wouldn't know that they're in middle school.
[03:48.6] You would think that they were adults for the sophistication of what they provide.
[03:52.8] And they have amazing business ideas.
[03:55.3] They propose businesses that I wouldn't want to buy from, that my family would want to buy from.
[04:00.2] So where else is that happening in U.S. classrooms? [do not use: names a place; NFTE wants national, evergreen cuts]
[04:04.1] I don't see it happening anywhere else but in NFTE classrooms and that's why we are working so hard to continue to expand throughout the nation and throughout the world and to bring more of what we do to even more students because they want it.
[04:18.9] Q: If you could bottle one moment from today to show policymakers, what would it be?
[04:24.9] If I could bottle one moment today to show policymakers, I would show them nothing more than what those three students did when they got up and they each in very different ways presented fantastic business plans.
[04:39.7] We had a young learner who presented in Spanish.
[04:43.0] That was fantastic.
[04:44.4] That's an asset.
[04:45.5] It showed people that he can work not only with entrepreneurship ideas but he can work bilingually.
[04:52.1] By the way, he also did a fantastic job fielding questions and doing them really well.
[04:57.3] So the fact that a student stood up there, was interrogated on the rigor of his business and stood up to that interrogation is something that I would want to see a district administrator or a school administrator see.
[20:00.3] I think it's ultimately relevant to sustaining our democracy, our society, because when you have people operating businesses that serve a community, you have many things.
[20:14.6] You have an entity that is providing something of value to the community.
[20:20.5] It is economic activity that benefits not just the business owner, but all the people who are connected to what that business owner needs.
[20:29.5] That helps sustain the community.
[20:31.6] You also create relationships.
[20:34.3] You create relationships with your customers.
[20:37.0] You create relationships with the families who come and discover your business.
[20:42.1] And so there's a whole human dimension that also creates the social fabric of communities.
[20:48.4] Entrepreneurship does that too.
[20:59.2] It's important to measure the economic impact of programs like NFTE because, well, first of all, we're entrepreneurship.
[21:07.4] So if we aren't measuring our business metrics, then we wouldn't be very good, would we?
[21:11.5] So we're pretty committed to that idea.
[21:13.5] But of course, people want to know that a program is not only providing a meaningful experience to a learner, but that it's also providing an effective experience to a learner.
[21:26.3] Learning can be measured.
[21:27.5] We all know that.
[21:28.8] Literacy, numeracy can and should be measured.
[21:33.2] Knowing where you are in terms of being a literate and financially literate person is essential to operating in life.
[21:41.2] So programs like ours that make a real effort to measure that type of learning are providing something valuable to the student, to the teacher, to the school, to the state policymakers who want to know how students are doing.
[21:53.9] So for those reasons, it's important.
[21:56.8] But measurement goes beyond and can go beyond the traditional way of looking at measurement.
[22:02.1] At NFTE, we pioneered the Entrepreneurial Mindset Index, which measures things that most people believe can't be measured but actually can be measured.
[22:11.5] They include things like the ability to manage risk, the ability to spot opportunities, the ability to problem-side, the ability to collaborate.
[22:22.3] We have designed scientifically valid.
[22:27.3] We have designed scientifically validated assessments that measure these capabilities.
[22:33.0] We call them entrepreneurial mindset capabilities.
[22:35.7] There are eight of them.
[22:37.1] And we're the only organization in the world, as far as I know, that really attempts to ascertain what all of our students are doing in this regard.
[22:47.6] This is next generation assessment when you think about it because, once again, we're living in a world where AI can read the document for you.
[22:57.8] It can analyze the spreadsheet of financials for you.
[23:01.5] But you also need to have creative capabilities.
[23:05.2] You need to work with other people.
[23:07.1] You need to look at the world around you and see if there is an opportunity out there that can help you or if there's something out there that you should be cautious about.
[23:15.2] AI can't do any of that.
[23:17.5] But the NFTE program does that.
[23:19.1] And that's another way that we can cultivate skills and also measure through sound assessment and 21st century assessment.
[23:44.5] I hope that people take away from this new analysis the idea that entrepreneurship is about so, so much more than just one person starting one business.
[23:55.3] I really encourage people who read this report and who really think about what NFTE does to recognize that we are empowering individuals.
[24:04.5] We are empowering families by creating economic lifelines for individuals to provide family prosperity.
[24:12.5] We are also providing and cultivating people who can be real emblems in their community by setting up businesses, by staying in their community, by investing and reinvigorating their community.
[24:27.6] Look at what is happening in the United States today.
[24:32.2] We are finding our way on so many things.
[24:35.7] We are divided on so many things.
[24:38.3] But I can't think of a single person I know or who I've ever talked to who has said, my community shouldn't be stronger.
[24:47.8] There should be fewer businesses.
[24:50.4] There should be less opportunity.
[24:53.5] NFTE provides opportunity.
[24:55.8] It provides a direct practical pathway for a young person to start and sustain a business with real educational knowledge about how to do it.
[25:04.5] And it provides a pathway for people to benefit themselves, their families, and their communities through that total effort.
[25:11.0] That is the magic of entrepreneurship.
[25:12.8] It is so rich.
[25:28.0] One of the things about the nonprofit field and the education field is that it's often fragmented.
[25:33.8] There are many organizations that work on many good things.
[25:38.6] And most of them, most of us, do it in this little pocket.
[25:43.8] And we do it for a while.
[25:46.1] And because the nonprofit model is not necessarily always the strongest business model, sometimes those organizations go away.
[25:56.7] They don't always prosper.
[25:58.7] The whole organizational fragmentation of the education sector and the nonprofit sector is a limiting factor in our collective effectiveness.
[26:08.0] So at NFTE a few years ago, we launched our CEO coalition of entrepreneurship education organizations, which banded together and does band together, going to Capitol Hill and the state legislatures to evangelize on behalf of the cause of entrepreneurship education. [do not use: names a place; NFTE wants national, evergreen cuts]
[26:29.6] What we saw was that policymakers, stakeholders, people from all different states across the country are really interested in what we have to do.
[26:39.3] And they like the fact that we are working in coalition together now to speak as one voice, that we're not competitors.
[26:46.5] We are actually colleagues believing in a common philosophy and working in a more coordinated way now to be able to elevate entrepreneurship education faster.
[26:57.2] Because right now we need to be doing more to elevate entrepreneurship education.
[27:03.6] American education needs a boost right now. [do not use: names a place; NFTE wants national, evergreen cuts]
[27:06.7] It needs some new ideas.
[27:09.0] And right now we have close to 10 or a dozen organizations like NFTE that under our leadership are now advancing this charge.
[27:19.3] I think we can take it a step further.
